title: Trees can’t run
content:
That changes everything. This is the spot, your spot, a spot worth protecting. Trees understand the power of the neighborhood and the value of good neighbors.

Trees can’t be anonymous, and they succeed by standing tall and sticking it out. Trees do better in a forest, surrounded by other trees.

And trees think in long time frames, because now keeps changing but later is the actual urgency.

Trees are mortal. And so generations are the actual long game. Fires and floods will come and go, but the seeds spread and flourish.

As humans, we often underestimate the gift of new decisions, new locations and the ability to quit and move on.

And just as often, we miss the chance to plant roots and stand for something.

HT to [Lisa Gansky](https://gansky.org/).

title: A Cross-Species Same-Sex Love Story
content:
Love is a many splendored thing. Powerful bonds can form where and when you least expect them. For instance, in the Ethiopian highlands between a black and white spotted bull and a tawny male donkey.

Recently, field scientists documented a kind of love affair between the two herd animals, who grazed together on a rocky plateau outside the village of Debre Libanos in a region known as Oromia, the breadbasket of the Horn of Africa. Over a period of weeks, the hoofed pair copulated dozens of times, nipped, licked, and nuzzled each other, and generally hung close during grazing time in open pasture and under the succulent shade of Sycamore trees.

**Read more: “**[**Why Are So Many Animals Homosexual**](https://nautil.us/why-are-so-many-animals-homosexual-235815)**?”**

When the team of scientists brought the story back home to Italy, their students decided to name the bull and the ass after characters in Homer’s epic poetry: The four-year-old bull, a species of humped cattle with drooping ears, was named Achilles, after a Greek warrior from _The Iliad_. His buddy, a nine-year-old domestic donkey, was named Patroclo, after Achilles’ dearest companion and fellow soldier in the war against Troy.

While Homer doesn’t explicitly describe the pair as lovers in _The Iliad_, same-sex relationships were integral to the ancient Greek world and later authors interpreted their intimate relationship as a romantic or sexual one. “Their deep attachment is central to the story” of _The Iliad_, wrote Elisabetta Palagi, an Italian evolutionary biologist from the Università di Pisa in Toscana, Italy, who was part of the team in Ethiopia, in an email.

Likewise, the story of our donkey and our bull.

The donkey-bull bond came to the scientists’ attention accidentally, while they were studying a primate known as the bleeding-heart monkey, which has distinctive hairless red patches on its chest and is native to the Ethiopian highlands. After the scientists observed the first tryst between the Achilles and Patroclo, they set out to document the interspecies romance in a methodical way.

Over a period of less than two weeks in March of 2026, the scientists made eight separate observations, and recorded the details of 51 mountings, the majority of which involved copulation, as well as other friendly behavior between the two animals. They [published](https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(26)01230-3) their results today in _Current Biology_.

When local herders noticed the keen interest the scientists were taking in the bull-donkey affair, they offered a bit of back story. Achilles and Patrocolo never spent the night together, as Achille was housed with another adult bull, a cow, and a calf, while Patroclo was housed with two other male donkeys. The two animals belong to different herds, and only interacted during daily shared pasture time, which, depending on the particular day, might include 3-6 bulls, 3-7 cows, 3 male donkeys, and 2-7 female donkeys.

Standard explanations for same-sex cross-species relationships between animals—which have been observed but are rare—tend to be somewhat uncharitable. Scientists have proposed that they may be the result of sexual coercion, mistaken identity or limited access to opposite sex or same species partners.

But none of these explanations hold for Achilles and Patroclo, Palagi told me. They had plenty of access to other potential partners from their own species, of both sexes. And when Achille mounted Patroclo, the donkey never kicked or resisted. On the contrary, Patroclo was an active participant in their encounters, pressing his haunches back toward Achille and nipping at him. “The recurring feature was the close association between sexual behaviour and friendly social contact,” said Palagi.

Why would a bull and a male donkey want to mate? Palagi speculates that the bond between the two animals probably helped with stress and offered reward. “A preferred partner might provide opportunities for rewarding physical contact, social support, or reduced tension,” she wrote. “Sexual interactions could themselves be rewarding and encourage the animals to continue seeking each other’s company.” The scientists did not test these hypotheses, however. They also don’t know which came first: Did the donkey and the bull begin as friends, then become friends with benefits, or did they feel sexual attraction from the start?

Domestication may have had something to do with it, by “altering social environments, opportunities for interspecific interactions, and behavioural flexibility,” the study authors wrote. Or it’s possible the pair’s behavior emerged “as a consequence of the social bonding systems of the two species.”

Other donkeys, at least, did not share Patrocolo’s affection for Achilles’ advances: In the only other two instances in which Achille attempted to mount another donkey, they showed clear signs of aversion, flattening their ears and making threatening facial expressions. None of the other animals in the herd engaged in cross-species mounting, either, and the only other time another bull attempted to mount Achilles he actively rejected it.

After the study was over and the scientists departed, Achille and Patroclo were separated. Grass was no longer available where they had been grazing together, so their owners set them to pasture in different fields. Palagi wonders what would happen if they were reunited. Would they remember one another? Would they pick up where they left off? We may never know. In matters of the heart, it is often impossible to tell what the future holds. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Can Whales Sing with Their Mouths Full?
content:
The most abundant whale species in the waters off southwest Australia is a subspecies of the blue whale: the pygmy blue whale (_Balaenoptera musculus brevicauda_)_._ Yet, despite being more common than other species, they’re endangered under an Australian conservation ruling, failing to recover fully after commercial whaling was banned in 1979.

Pygmy blue whales are hard to spot because they’re smaller than other blue whales and spend most of their time below the surface, filter-feeding on krill with their baleen. But a [new study](https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rsos/article/13/10/260954/483903/Pygmy-blue-whale-feeding-drives-greater-nocturnal) published in the journal _Royal Society Open Science_ provides a method for monitoring pygmy whale feeding activities without needing to see them at all.

**Read more:****“**[**The Cold War’s Accidental Whale Observatory**](https://nautil.us/the-cold-wars-accidental-whale-observatory-1281682)**”**

Led by doctoral student Andrew Davenport from Curtin’s Centre for Marine Science and Technology, the study explored the relationship between periods of feeding behavior and whale song since blue whales make sounds while they’re feeding, [such as “D-calls”](https://www.int-res.com/journals/meps/articles/meps330269) that slide from higher to lower frequency.

Their songs were analyzed from recordings collected passively over three months, with nothing attached to the whales that might alter their natural behavior. The researchers found that this Australian population of pygmy blue whales sang less when they were actively feeding during the daytime, regardless of whether they were in the foraging regions of Perth Canyon, Midwest, or Northwest.

“Just as we can’t talk while we’re eating, pygmy blue whales appear to have less time available to sing while they’re feeding,” Davenport explained in a [press release](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1149677).

And so, whale songs could serve as a proxy for direct monitoring of feeding behavior—at least for pygmy blue whales. Without tagging or observing the whales, researchers can record their daytime singing and assume they’re foraging during the quiet periods. “By listening to when they sing more at night than during the day, we can infer when whales in an area are likely to be feeding,” added Davenport.

Which, of course, will serve as a bountiful feast of data for him and his team. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Meds Are Often the Go-to for Dementia Patients. Is There a Better Way?
content:
_[This story](https://knowablemagazine.org/content/article/health-disease/2026/can-non-drug-approaches-ease-lives-dementia-patients) was originally published by_[Knowable Magazine](https://knowablemagazine.org/content/article/society/2026/prehistory-lost-threads)_._

After Bobby Tweed moved into a Tennessee nursing home, the spirited 78-year-old with dementia grew listless and withdrawn. Tweed, a gentle man who his daughter says “never hit anybody in his whole life,” was suddenly labeled “agitated” after a scuffle with another resident.

In reality, Tweed was suffering from a common, treatable urinary tract infection, a physical condition well known to trigger temporary delirium and behavioral changes in dementia patients. Doctors treated him for the infection, but facility staff still turned to powerful psychotropic drugs that, according to a [wrongful death lawsuit](https://www.aarp.org/health/drugs-supplements/wrongful-death-lawsuit-nursing-home/), were administered without his family’s knowledge or consent.

The medications achieved what they were meant to do: They stopped behaviors caregivers found difficult.

“They just kept him drugged up so they didn’t have to deal with him,” says his daughter, Robin Tweed Keller. Tweed was left in a stupor so deep that family members who came to visit at different times of the day could not wake him up.

As her father retreated behind a chemical haze, Keller was left wondering whether what staff called “agitation” was really a language that no one had tried hard enough to understand.

That possibility is at the center of an ongoing struggle in dementia care. While memory loss is the hallmark of dementia, the disease is [also marked by troubling changes in behavior](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24635665/) — such as aggression, shouting, irritability and depression. These symptoms are frequently treated with antipsychotics, despite longstanding warnings about serious risks of their use in older adults with dementia.

A pair of 2026 [federal watchdog reports](https://oig.hhs.gov/reports/work-plan/browse-work-plan-projects/srs-e-26-006/) indicate that the practice remains deeply entrenched in US nursing homes. The Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General found that facilities [still use the medications](https://oig.hhs.gov/reports/all/2026/nursing-homes-inappropriate-use-of-antipsychotic-drugs-poses-a-risk-to-residents/) as “chemical restraints,” often without first attempting required non-pharmacological interventions. Investigators also detailed how some facilities hide their true prescribing rates by [inappropriately diagnosing residents with schizophrenia](https://oig.hhs.gov/reports/all/2026/nursing-homes-inappropriately-diagnosed-residents-with-schizophrenia-to-mask-the-misuse-of-antipsychotic-drugs/), a condition excluded from federal quality measures tracking antipsychotic use.

“It’s showing that the problems continue to exist in full force in nursing homes, and we still have not solved this problem, and we still need to do more,” says Lori Smetanka, executive director of the National Consumer Voice for Quality Long-Term Care.

The issue extends beyond care homes to older adults receiving care in a range of settings, including those living in residential facilities and those remaining in their own homes. In all, [national prescribing data](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapsychiatry/article-abstract/2842203) show that antipsychotic use among adults 65 and older increased by nearly 52 percent between 2015 and 2024, with long-term use (defined as more than four months) rising by almost 65 percent.

The analysis included more than 8 million older Americans who received at least one antipsychotic prescription, reflecting the broad use of drugs whose benefits and risks remain hotly debated.

In response, many clinicians and advocates are pushing for a different approach. Rather than treating these dementia-related actions as symptoms to be suppressed, they are instead describing them as expressions of unmet needs.

“Behaviors can have meaning to people with dementia,” says Jennifer Watt, a geriatrician at the University of Toronto and a coauthor of a [2026 article on the subject](https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-clinpsy-061724-085912) in the _Annual Review of Clinical Psychology_.

As language deteriorates, people may express themselves through actions instead of words. A person wandering the kitchen may be hungry or thirsty but unable to articulate it. Someone resisting a bath may be reacting to cold water or pain from arthritis. “It’s actually just people trying to communicate a need in the only way that they are able to at that point in time,” Watt says.

**Poorly Defined Symptoms**

Nearly every person diagnosed with dementia — [an estimated 97 percent](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2932652/) — will eventually experience changes in mood, perception or behavior. “There are complexities of the neurodegenerative changes in the brain that fundamentally alter how the brain works,” says Watt. The precise mechanisms behind these manifestations remain poorly understood.

Some develop anxiety or depression. Others grow emotionally flat and withdrawn. Hallucinations and delusions may distort reality. Many develop what clinicians call “agitation,” a broad and imperfect term that can include pacing, restlessness, repetitive questions and sudden flashes of anger or even violence.

Clinicians often group these experiences under the umbrella of “behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia,” or BPSD.

For decades, nursing homes, hospitals and other residential care settings have [often responded with antipsychotic medications](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28617907/). Originally developed in the 1950s for schizophrenia, antipsychotics became widely used in dementia care to manage BPSD behaviors such as hallucinations, delusions, agitation and aggression — symptoms that can also occur in schizophrenia.

By the 1970s, federal investigators were already warning that nursing home residents were [being chemically restrained](https://www.aging.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/reports/rpt175.pdf). Reforms beginning in the 1980s helped to curb the use of older, “typical” antipsychotics, but a newer generation of “atypical” drugs, considered safer, soon took their place.

Then in the early 2000s, studies linked these [newer antipsychotics](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16505124/) in older adults with dementia to sharply increased risks of death, stroke, heart failure and accelerated cognitive decline. Mounting evidence of these and other [serious harms](https://www.bmj.com/content/385/bmj-2023-076268.long), including a heightened risk of bone fractures related to falls, prompted the US Food and Drug Administration to issue its strongest [“black box” warning](https://www.bmj.com/content/330/7497/922.4). Federal regulators introduced new oversight measures, including adding antipsychotic use to Medicare’s [public Five-Star Quality Rating System](https://www.cms.gov/medicare/health-safety-standards/certification-compliance/five-star-quality-rating-system), which tied a facility’s score to its prescribing rates.

Use declined, only to [rise again](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36272888/) during the Covid-19 pandemic, when staffing reached critical lows and family visits were restricted. Today, antipsychotic use remains substantial: Under a newly revised federal measure designed to capture prescribing more accurately, about [17 percent](https://www.cms.gov/files/document/qso-25-20-nh-revised-2025-09-10.pdf) of long-stay nursing home residents receive an antipsychotic.

A 2018 Human Rights Watch report on the misuse of antipsychotic drugs to quell disruptive behavior in elderly nursing home residents identified hundreds of US facilities in which more than 30 percent of residents had been prescribed the psychotropic drugs. _Credit: Human Rights Watch / CC BY-NC-ND_

Despite their widespread use, antipsychotics are only [marginally effective](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD013304_do-antipsychotic-medicines-reduce-agitated-behaviour-and-psychotic-symptoms-people-alzheimers) in treating the behavioral symptoms of dementia. Results from randomized controlled trials are frequently characterized as [weak](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34918337/); larger analyses suggest benefits [that are barely perceptible](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27133416/) compared with placebos. While these drugs are powerful sedatives that can make a person docile, experts say they do little to solve the actual distress the individual is experiencing.

“Instead of getting to the root problem and addressing the problem, we’re quieting them down,” says Smetanka. “And then that’s what leads to significant problems with their health and well-being.” On top of the medications’ direct risks, a resident who is sleepy or less responsive may move less and be less able to signal pain or a new illness.

**Best Practice vs. In Practice**

Medical guidelines generally recommend [trying non-drug approaches first](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0197457226001084) for behavioral symptoms of dementia. In practice, though, medications are often the default. Growing efforts to close that gap are rooted in the idea that behaviors in dementia can have “meaning” — that they may signal unmet needs rather than simply be symptoms to suppress.

Non-drug approaches range from personalized music playlists and walking programs to reminiscence therapy using old photographs and household objects. More specialized methods, such as one called Snoezelen therapy, use controlled light, sound, texture and scent to calm people experiencing sensory overload or deprivation.

Unlike antipsychotic medications, non-pharmacological interventions are generally considered low risk, though the evidence supporting their effectiveness remains mixed. Studies are often small, difficult to standardize and nearly impossible to blind in the way that drug trials are conducted.

Even so, some research has shown promising results. A review that pooled and assessed the findings of multiple studies, led by Watt, showed that [sensory-oriented approaches](https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/abs/10.7326/m19-0993) — such as music therapy, massage and outdoor activity — reduced agitation as well as or better than medications. She and her colleagues also found that exercise, cognitive stimulation and reminiscence therapy can relieve depression more effectively than antidepressants, which often perform little better than a placebo in patients with dementia.

Best practice is to first assess and manage any underlying causes, says Helen Kales, a geriatric psychiatrist and mental health services researcher at the University of California, Davis. The cause may be something as simple as too much noise, an unfamiliar routine, urinary tract infections or pain that the person can no longer describe.

Kales recalls a man with dementia who was brought to see her after his daughter said he had become increasingly “ornery” and “awful.” The apparent behavioral problem turned out to have a physical cause: He had a rotator cuff tear.

Not every case is so straightforward. Even caregivers committed to person-centered care often struggle to determine which interventions work best and how to sustain them in practice.

In 2024, Watt helped to develop [Canadian clinical practice guidelines](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38640961/) for the most common behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia. As part of that work, she and her team reviewed [dementia care guidelines](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33762262/) from around the world and found little agreement about best practices. “It’s not consistent,” says Watt, “which of course is really confusing and does not instill confidence in care providers.”

Caregivers also face practical barriers, including limited training and chronic understaffing. A certified nursing assistant may care for well over a dozen residents during a day shift, and far more in lower-staffed facilities, says Smetanka. Under those conditions, medication can be the quickest way to stabilize a situation. Studies consistently show that facilities with fewer workers [use antipsychotics at higher rates](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2818030). And annual [staff turnover](https://www.healthaffairs.org/doi/pdf/10.1377/hlthaff.2020.00957) rates ranging from 50 percent to as high as 100 percent at certain facilities make it hard for caregivers to know residents well enough to interpret their behavior.

“We’re just not structured to really handle the way these symptoms unfold,” says Kales.

Geriatric psychiatrists such as Helen Kales and others have developed suggestions for caregivers coping with common behavioral problems experienced by those with dementia. _Credit: Adapted from H.C. Kales et al / Journal of the American Geriatrics Society 2014/ Knowable Magazine_

Economic incentives reinforce the pattern. Antipsychotic medications are relatively inexpensive and typically covered by insurance, while non-pharmacological approaches require staffing and training that many facilities cannot sustain. According to a 2018 Human Rights Watch study, [some families report](https://www.hrw.org/report/2018/02/05/they-want-docile/how-nursing-homes-in-the-united-states-overmedicate-people-with) feeling pressured to agree to sedating medications, with facilities warning that a resident will be evicted or require an expensive 24-hour private nurse if they do not comply.

Industry groups often argue that staffing shortages and financial pressures leave facilities with few alternatives. But those constraints do not fully explain why some nursing homes rely more heavily on antipsychotics than others. “You do see pockets of progress,” says Smetanka. “There are a lot of places that do provide very good care for people with dementia, for residents with all kinds of needs, without inappropriately prescribing drugs to them in order to control their behavior. So, if they can do it, everybody else can do it too.”

What stands in the way is not always a belief that medication is the easier or cheaper option. The Human Rights Watch report found that nursing home staff often believed antipsychotics genuinely benefited residents. A 2017 Vanderbilt University study described caregiving staff feeling [morally obligated](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28575301/) to “give them something” when residents appeared distressed. Yet workers also noted dramatic improvements when residents were taken off the medications, including greater alertness, responsiveness and engagement in daily life.

To help caregivers respond to distressing behaviors without defaulting to medication, Kales led the development of the [DICE approach](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4707529/) — short for Describe, Investigate, Create and Evaluate. The first step asks caregivers to describe behavior in concrete terms rather than relying on catchall labels like “agitation.” Staff are trained to “play back the behavior, like a movie,” Kales says. They’re asked to note what happened, when, and under what circumstances.

Next comes investigation. Could the person be in pain? Constipated? Frightened by noise or confusion? The third step involves creating a plan tailored to the likely causes. That may mean simplifying routines, adjusting communication styles or introducing more meaningful activity. Finally, caregivers evaluate what worked and what did not.

“It’s really asking our teams to slow down before we make any reaction,” says Kelsey Burnham, a Michigan-based program director at Ascension Living, a nationwide senior living provider that implemented DICE across its locations earlier this year.

Burnham says the approach gives staff “a unifying language” for interpreting and responding to residents’ distress. “I think we’re so focused as an industry on what we can’t do that it really limits our thinking,” she says. “What’s not talked about as much ... is, what _can_ we do?”

The new framework has been adapted for home use, too. As a digital tool called WeCareAdvisor, it walks family members through the process of describing behaviors and identifying possible triggers. The app uses a database of roughly 1,000 [evidence-based strategies](https://www.ovid.com/jnls/alzheimerjournal/fulltext/10.1097/wad.0000000000000177~wecareadvisor-the-development-of-a-caregiver-focused) to suggest non-drug approaches that can be tried in different situations.

A randomized trial of 262 caregivers using the app found modest improvements in [caregiver distress and well-being](https://agsjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jgs.70637). But the tool did not significantly change the frequency or severity of behavioral symptoms over three months, leaving open questions about how much it can change day-to-day dementia care.

**Reverting to Medication**

Even as researchers continue to make the case for non-pharmacological approaches, broader industry trends may be steering care back toward medication.

Federal minimum staffing standards have already been [rolled back](https://www.hhs.gov/press-room/hhs-cleanup-federal-nursing-home-minimum-staffing-standards-rule-expands-access-rural-tribal-health-care.html). At the same time, a lobbying coalition known as Project PAUSE — backed by pharmaceutical companies and groups from the long-term care industry — is pressing federal regulators to [overhaul oversight](https://www.agingresearch.org/news/project-pause-urges-replacement-of-long-stay-antipsychotic-quality-measure-for-patients-with-neuropsychiatric-symptoms/) of antipsychotic prescribing. Among the coalition’s goals: removing the current antipsychotic measure from the federal nursing home rating system and replacing it with a system that would give facilities more leeway to justify prescribing.

Critics argue that the changes would undermine the few transparency safeguards available to families and regulators. “When you take away all those mechanisms, I would not be surprised if we saw the numbers increasing again,” says Smetanka.

[Studies](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11890954/) have also documented what researchers term a [“balloon effect”](https://www.aarp.org/caregiving/medical/psychotropic-medication-nursing-homes/) — as scrutiny of antipsychotics intensifies, prescribing shifts toward other sedating drugs, including opioids as well as [anticonvulsants](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2765053) that face less oversight.

Meanwhile, a new medication may complicate the conversation. In April 2026, the FDA [approved Auvelity](https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-non-antipsychotic-drug-treat-agitation-associated-dementia), a combination of dextromethorphan and bupropion, specifically for agitation associated with Alzheimer’s disease. The drug appears to be less sedating and potentially safer than many antipsychotics used in dementia care.

The Alzheimer’s Association, a nonprofit organization that funds Alzheimer’s and dementia research, [describes the decision](https://www.alz.org/news/2026/alzheimers-association-welcomes-fda-approval-treatment-for-agitation) as a significant expansion of options for patients and clinicians who have long faced limited and often risky choices for managing agitation.

Still, some experts worry. The rating scales used in drug trials can define “agitation” broadly, encompassing behaviors ranging from pacing and restlessness to yelling and aggression. Kales is concerned that a new, seemingly safer drug could encourage more behaviors to be swept under that label — and treated with medication.

“Sadly, this means more drugs and less person-centered care,” says Kales. “Why take the time to look for underlying causes when you can medicate?”

Even promising new treatments, advocates contend, cannot substitute for adequate staffing, caregiver training and individualized care. For many families, these are not abstract policy debates, but daily questions about dignity, safety and whether their loved ones will be treated as people with needs and emotions rather than disruptions to be managed.

It is a reality that Robin Keller lived through with her father, Bobby Tweed. Years after his death — officially attributed on his death certificate to an interaction between the drugs he was given — she still wrestles with the “100 ifs” of what she might have done differently.

Dementia had slowly chipped away at the vibrant practical joker who spent his retirement volunteering with the fire department and cooking hamburgers at local horse shows. But for Keller, the deeper tragedy of his final weeks was that a flawed system had chemically shuttered what remained of his spirit before his body gave out. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

# Is Sleeping in on the Weekends Bad for Your Heart?

A new study links sleep regularity to cardiovascular health

[JC](https://nautil.us/author/jake-currie)

By [Jake Currie](https://nautil.us/author/jake-currie)

7:00 AM CST on November 2, 2026

[Add Nautilus to Google](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=nautil.us)

![Image 4](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/2026/11/shutterstock_2532074937.jpg?w=2880)

Daylight Saving Time is now over, which means you probably enjoyed an extra hour of sleep over the weekend. Unfortunately, even a welcome disruption of your sleep cycle may be bad for your heart, at least according to preliminary research to be presented later this week at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions.

A team of medical researchers led by Nguyen Minh Tuan Viet of Harvard Medical school analyzed health data from over 10,300 adults enrolled in the National Institutes of Health’s “All of Us” Research Program. As part of that program, these subjects were outfitted with Fitbits that recorded their sleep activity for six months, including when they went to bed and woke up, how much of their slumber was spent in light versus deep sleep, and the number of sleep cycles they experienced during the night. Altogether, the dataset included more than one million hours of sleep.

**Read more: “[How the Heat is Messing with Your Sleep](https://nautil.us/how-the-heat-is-messing-with-your-sleep-1284501)”**

The team found that it was changes to the sleep schedule that showed the biggest impacts on heart health. Those who experienced shifts in their sleep schedules had a roughly 20 percent higher risk of serious heart events, including heart attack, stroke, and heart failure. Every 29-minute change in how much sleep participants got—in either direction—was associated with a 24-percent increase in risk for these adverse outcomes. (For those keeping score, that’s roughly three hits of the snooze button.)

It’s a somewhat surprising finding. After all, we’re used to headlines linking too little sleep to poorer health. This investigation suggests _any change_ in our schedules could be detrimental to our hearts. And it’s particularly bad news for those who like to catch a few extra Z’s on the weekends. “Sleep irregularity is often due to weekends,” Viet explained in a [statement](https://newsroom.heart.org/news/is-a-consistent-sleep-schedule-important-to-heart-health). “We get to sleep a little bit later on a Friday night; or people have shift work. This may not be good for your heart health.”

So what can we do?

The answer, per the researchers, is to stick to a stricter sleep schedule. Or as Viet put it, “While we often focus on getting a full eight hours of sleep every night, having a regular sleep schedule—consistent bedtimes, wake times, and sleep duration from night to night is a practical, actionable step anyone can take that may help protect their heart and blood vessels.” ![Image 8](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Is There Anything Left in the Dream of Cold Fusion?
content:
![Image 1: Qualia: Essays that go where curiosity leads](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2050/01/QUALIA-Banner-WITH-SPACER-1-1720x223.webp)

C old fusion: Now there’s an idea I hadn’t thought about in a while. It came back onto my radar in spring 2026. I had written an article on how scientists tend to be risk averse, and [Huw Price (opens a new tab)](https://prce.hu/w/), a philosopher at Trinity College at the University of Cambridge, responded to it on Bluesky, citing a paper he’d recently co-authored on attitudes toward cold fusion. He thinks scientists have been overly dismissive not only of cold fusion, but also of the _claim_ that they have been overly dismissive of cold fusion. As if to prove his point, a journal had just rejected his paper. I’ve long admired Price’s work on the nature of time and causation, so I was intrigued.

When the cold-fusion controversy erupted in 1989, I was in the middle of backpacking off the grid for six months. (You could do that back then.) By the time I caught up on the news, it was over. In March, two chemists had called a press conference to announce a simple tabletop experiment that released too much energy to be a mere chemical reaction. They said it had to be nuclear: hydrogen nuclei fusing to form helium. It promised limitless clean, cheap power. Physicists were stunned. That sort of thing wasn’t supposed to be possible under such pedestrian conditions. Politicians proclaimed the end of all our energy woes. But then labs across the globe tried to replicate the experiment and couldn’t, and an almighty takedown ensued. The whole thing only lasted a few months. Not having experienced the episode in real time, and being a contrarian by nature, I initially sympathized with the plucky maverick scientists. But then I read about their rookie mistakes, their fudging of a crucial graph, and their threats of lawsuits against skeptics. Experiments that initially corroborated the results were retracted, in one case amid indications of deliberate spiking with fake fusion products.

Although cold fusion was a pathological case, fusion in general has been a graveyard of dreams. I grew up on the dream it evoked. Whether it occurs at room temperature, as it was supposed to have done in the cold-fusion episode, or at center-of-the-sun temperatures, as in conventional thermonuclear reactors (and bombs), fusion doesn’t require strip-mining (and disposing of) uranium or escorting oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz. All you would need, ideally, is a bit of seawater. Fascinated, I once built a “fusor” in my basement based on an [article (opens a new tab)](https://makezine.com/projects/nuclear-fusor/) in _Make_ magazine. Fusors are real, the one legitimate tabletop fusion technology. In them, a high voltage creates a hot plasma that smashes nuclei together. My unit didn’t achieve fusion, but with work it could have, although it would have produced negligible power. I loved showing guests its glowing purple plasma, but the more I learned about fusion, the more a sense of disillusionment grew in me. A couple of years later, a friend at a private fusion company gave me a tour of an actual experimental fusion reactor. It was complex and costly. So much for cheap. It produced intense, deadly neutron radiation. So much for clean. And it required tritium fuel, which does not occur naturally and has to be manufactured. So much for just a bit of seawater.

So how did a nice philosopher like Price get mixed up in a business like this? Over Zoom, he explained that his interest dates to 2011, when he and other luminaries were hatching the idea for the Center for the Study of Existential Risk. This research group frets over nuclear winter, engineered bioweapons, massive volcanic eruptions, and artificial intelligence takeover — it rang that alarm bell long before it became fashionable. Price told me he saw parallels between doomsday scenarios and cold fusion. They may seem improbable, and studying them is a lonely or even fringe activity, yet the consequences are huge, so we should give more weight to them than might strictly seem warranted.

I’m all for open-mindedness, but Price’s argument troubled me. There must be a thousand other anomalous phenomena that are as likely to be real as cold fusion and, if they are, to transform the world. Why focus on this one? The only reason we are talking about cold fusion at all is that we were lied to in 1989. The initial mistruth created a kind of psychological anchoring effect, causing us to entertain a possibility that we otherwise wouldn’t have. It is as if I said I saw Bigfoot in my backyard, then confessed I hadn’t, but people started holding annual cryptozoological conferences nearby anyway. I found it jarring that a deception could conjure an entire academic research program. How is this any different from the antivax movement, which also started with data that turned out to be faked and should have just packed up once that became known?

But having started down this rabbit hole, I figured I might as well keep going. Price suggested I talk to [Matt Trevithick (opens a new tab)](https://leitmotif.vc/team/matt-trevithick).

![Image 2](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/QUALIA-Separator-2.webp)

Trevithick is a co-founder of Leitmotif, a venture capital firm in Palo Alto. I don’t normally speak to venture capitalists, but I quickly saw that his approach aligns with Price’s. Trevithick wants to usher in the fusion age and supports a range of technologies that might make it happen. In our conversation, he also had a very Silicon Valley tendency to keep addressing me by name.

A decade ago, while working at Google, Trevithick organized a project to reevaluate cold fusion, culminating in a [_Nature_ paper (opens a new tab)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-019-1256-6) in 2019. It didn’t find any unexpected nuclear reactions or other anomalies, but that wasn’t the only goal. Trevithick said the 1989 debacle had cast a pall over certain research topics that perhaps shouldn’t be so easily dismissed. For instance, cold fusioneers used the element palladium in their experiments, and it has a wondrous ability to absorb hydrogen like a sponge, an ability that is no less wondrous for its association with a scientific wild goose chase. Trevithick sought to lift this taboo, and he said the project ultimately produced 28 academic papers on hydrogenated metals and other phenomena. “George,” he said. “We destigmatized a field.”

So I went through the references in the _Nature_ paper and looked up topics I might not have given a second thought to before. The one that captivated me was muon-catalyzed fusion. I recognized it as the original meaning of the term “cold fusion” before it was co-opted by the 1989 studies. As I unpacked what it meant, I discovered a [lively research program (opens a new tab)](https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/open.substack.com/pub/criticalopalescence/p/honey-i-shrunk-the-atoms?r=2cb3jc&utm_campaign=post&utm_medium=web&showWelcomeOnShare=true__;!!DSb-azq1wVFtOg!SWx0WqVtefY0mqGm8E4CSR2dY0c2v1fAVyuxUimKn4T8xHd2mcuA24gh0i_9XmBcABbCCfer60O-3oK3Xfid$) within physics that creates exotic breeds of atoms and molecules, sometimes to try to fuse them together, but more broadly to search for new fundamental laws of nature.

Still wary of the dubious reputation of cold fusion, I reached out to physicists I trusted to learn more. One was [Cătălina Curceanu (opens a new tab)](https://inspirehep.net/authors/993589) of the Italian National Institute for Nuclear Physics near Rome. I had visited her three years before to see her experiments testing the foundations of quantum mechanics. She gently reminded me that she had told me about exotic atoms back then, too. I guess I was so focused on her other work that I failed to follow up. “It’s a whole world to discover,” she said. “Sometimes I call them ‘genetically modified atoms,’ but I stopped doing that because, you know.”

The core idea that builds to muon-catalyzed fusion is simple. Ordinary atoms consist of a positively charged nucleus orbited by negatively charged electrons. But there’s no reason they have to be electrons. Other negatively charged particles serve just as well. In the [Standard Model of particle physics](https://www.quantamagazine.org/a-new-map-of-the-standard-model-of-particle-physics-20201022/), the electron has a sibling called the muon that can stand in for it. Physicists have also swapped in particles from other families, such as kaons, pions, and Xi baryons. They have even created hybrids of matter and antimatter, in which a nucleus containing protons is orbited by negatively charged antiprotons. In short, you can have regular hydrogen, muonic hydrogen, kaonic hydrogen, antiprotonic hydrogen, and so on.

“That’s like a new periodic table,” said [Daniel Swetz (opens a new tab)](https://www.nist.gov/people/daniel-swetz), an experimental physicist at the National Institute of Standards and Technology in Boulder, Colorado, who builds ultraprecise detectors to measure radiation emitted by these exotic atoms. “You’re almost building it out in the third dimension.”

The main difference in these exotic atoms is that the electron substitutes are much heavier. A muon is 207 times as massive as an electron; an antiproton, 1,800 times. According to quantum mechanics, every object is ultimately wavelike, and the greater its mass, the shorter its wavelength. Consequently, a muonic atom is as much as 207 times smaller than its vanilla counterpart, depending on the chemical isotope; an antiprotonic atom, as much as 1,800 times smaller. When physicists want to get across the scale of atoms, they often compare the nucleus to a marble and the whole atom to a football stadium around that marble. With antiprotonic atoms, however, the atom is not a football stadium, but just a football.

“The whole system is collapsed down,” said [Nancy Paul (opens a new tab)](https://www.lkb.fr/exoticions/about-the-team/people/nancy-paul/), a physicist at the Kastler Brossel Laboratory in Paris. She is exploring using even heavier negatively charged particles to shrink atoms still further. “It’s so rare in physics, especially nowadays, where you get something where nothing has been done.”

Shrinking atoms intensifies the electric field within them. According to Coulomb’s law, which is the electric counterpart of Newton’s law of gravity, the electric field strengthens as the inverse square of distance. For a kaonic or antiprotonic atom, then, it scales up a millionfold. That provides a stress test of a central pillar of modern physics, quantum electrodynamics (QED), or how electromagnetism behaves at the quantum level. “It is the strongest Coulomb field that you can create in the lab to probe QED,” Paul said.

In fact, it breaches the so-called Schwinger limit, the threshold at which quantum effects go berserk and empty space becomes unstable. Particles begin to materialize spontaneously out of nothingness. “You’re boiling the vacuum with the stronger field,” she said. Physicists predicted this particle effervescence in the 1930s and have yet to observe it directly, but they have discerned a closely related phenomenon using exotic atoms. In spring 2026, Curceanu and her colleagues did so using [kaonic fluorine (opens a new tab)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.19387) that was experiencing an electric field above the Schwinger limit.

Shrunken atoms open a window into other aspects of fundamental physics, too. The muons, kaons, or other electron substitutes orbit the atomic nucleus so tightly that they become sensitive to its interior structure. This was how the [radius of the proton](https://www.quantamagazine.org/physicists-finally-nail-the-protons-size-and-hope-dies-20190911/) was measured in 2019. Like a miniature planet, the nucleus can be layered, with an outer crust or “skin” of neutrons. “You have a really beautiful microscope of seeing what’s happening at these neutron skins,” Paul said. Shrunken atoms might allow researchers to pick up on wholly new physics, such as deviations from Newtonian gravity or the existence of particles beyond the Standard Model. “We are looking into unknown physics at the extreme precision limit,” Curceanu said. “It’s complementary to extreme high energy.”

Even creating these atoms inverts the intuitions of particle physics. CERN’s flagship instrument, the [Large Hadron Collider](https://www.quantamagazine.org/tag/large-hadron-collider/), revs up particles almost to light speed to initiate those high-energy interactions. Paul’s team instead relies on a lesser-known machine called the Antiproton Decelerator that slows particles to a crawl, so that they become able to infiltrate atoms instead of blasting them apart. In some ways, it’s a harder job. “Acceleration is easier than deceleration,” said [Lars Jørgensen (opens a new tab)](https://ch.linkedin.com/in/lars-varming-j%C3%B8rgensen-a843411), an experimentalist at CERN who helped to develop the decelerator.

It took him an hour to walk me through the stages of the process. The system creates antiprotons and gradually bleeds off their energy. Some stages act on entire clumps of particles to slow them down, while others act within a clump to keep it from spreading out. One technique is to flood the chamber with electrons, which cool the antiprotons like so many ice cubes. Magnetic fields and an extreme vacuum — so extreme that no pressure gauge can measure it — ensure that the antiprotons don’t prematurely encounter ordinary protons, which would annihilate both. In 2021, CERN began operating the Extra Low Energy Antiproton ring, or ELENA, to do the final braking. Creating and slowing other electron surrogates such as muons is easier because they don’t pose the annihilation challenge.

At that point, inserting these particles into atoms is easy. Atoms are surprisingly klutzy when it comes to their electrons. They are apt to lose them for all sorts of reasons, and exotic-atom formation exploits this tendency, with the novelty that the lost electron is replaced with an incoming particle. If the atom was originally in its lowest possible energy state, the new arrival immediately defines a new set of energy levels, like a fire-escape ladder that suddenly descends. The atom drops through the newly established energy levels. In the process it ejects all its remaining electrons and emits a series of X-rays.

The atom eventually stabilizes again, but not for long. In an antiprotonic atom, the antiproton reaches such a tight orbit that it touches the nucleus and annihilates. In other types of exotic atoms, the electron substitute quickly decays. Muons last a mere 2 microseconds, and other species are even more fleeting. But during these truncated lifespans, exotic atoms can even form short-lived molecules.

I heard about them from [Shinji Okada (opens a new tab)](https://www.chubu.ac.jp/english/get-to-know-us/1637/), a physicist at Chubu University in Japan. In spring 2026, his team used Swetz’s detectors and the Japan Proton Accelerator Research Complex to measure the structure of [muonic hydrogen molecules (opens a new tab)](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/sciadv.aed3321), with the hydrogen taking the form of the isotope deuterium — the first direct measurement of X-rays emitted by such molecules. When they were smashed into molecules consisting of two ordinary hydrogen atoms, the muonic atoms implanted themselves within those molecules and assimilated one of their hydrogens. This created what Okada called a “matryoshka molecule” — an exotic molecule embedded inside a larger ordinary molecule.

And this brings us back to the idea that got me started: muon-catalyzed fusion. In other experiments, when the exotic molecule reaches its final configuration, it is so compact that the two hydrogens fuse almost instantly. This process happens at room temperature, so in that sense it is “cold,” but otherwise it’s very different from the 1989 experiment — not least because it really does happen. The muon is typically ejected, freeing it to create a new exotic atom and restart the cycle; thus, the muon is acting as a catalyst, a nuclear matchmaker. If it could repeat the trick 300 times or more, the process would produce more energy than it consumed. Most physicists doubt it could reach 300, but Okada said he and his team don’t entirely rule it out. Still, the particles released by the fusion reactions could be harvested to synthesize medical isotopes or process nuclear waste from fission reactors. “Even without reaching energy breakeven, muon-catalyzed fusion could be useful,” Okada said.

And that’s important because, although physicists first observed muon-catalyzed fusion in the 1950s, few studied it, deeming it a mere curiosity. What good could it be if it couldn’t generate energy? The main development of recent years has not been a breakthrough on muon recycling but a realization that we don’t need any such breakthrough.

I think that carries a general lesson for evaluating developments in science. What makes headlines — Abundant energy! Humanity saved! — isn’t what you should focus on. Instead, ask: Will this research program be interesting, even if the main claim falls short? Is it an all-or-nothing gamble on a single result, or a portal into a wider area of science?

Cold fusion, as presented to the world in 1989, failed this test. Those two chemists never articulated why their experiment might be interesting even if it didn’t herald energy salvation. That task fell to Trevithick 30 years later, when his project showed that a cold-fusion type of experiment, if pursued on its own merits, could reveal fascinating material properties.

Muon-catalyzed fusion passes the test, because exotic atoms and molecules enrich our view of the universe even if they never produce a watt of electricity. The scientists I spoke to were clearly not driven by any expectation of fame and fortune, but rather by curiosity and wonder. “Isn’t that remarkable?” Okada told me. “Atomic, molecular, and nuclear physics all come together in a single reaction cycle. That interplay is what has captivated me.”

title: Trial, Triumph, and the Art of the Possible: The Moving Story Behind Beethoven’s “Ode to Joy,” a Lifetime of Sorrow in the Making
content:
“Day by day I am approaching the goal which I apprehend but cannot describe,” **Ludwig van Beethoven** (December 16, 1770–March 26, 1827) wrote to his boyhood friend, [rallying his own resilience](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/09/19/beethoven-take-fate-by-the-throat/) as he began losing his hearing. A year later, shortly after completing his _Second Symphony_, he sent his brothers a stunning letter about [the joy of suffering overcome](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/02/08/beethoven-romain-rolland-letters/), in which he resolved:

> Ah! how could I possibly quit the world before bringing forth all that I felt it was my vocation to produce?

That year, he began — though he did not yet know it, as we never do — the long gestation of what would become not only his greatest creative and spiritual triumph, not only a turning point in the history of music that revolutionized the symphony and planted the seed of the pop song, but an eternal masterwork of the supreme human art: making meaning out of chaos, beauty out of sorrow.

Across the epochs, “Ode to Joy” rises vast and eternal, transcending all of spacetime and at the same time compacting it into something so intimate, so immediate, that nothing seems to exist outside this singularity of all-pervading possibility. Inside its total drama, a total tranquility; inside its revolt, an oasis of refuge. The story of its making is as vitalizing as the masterpiece itself — or, rather, its story is the very reason for its vitality.

[![Image 1](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/beethoven_mahler.jpg?resize=680%2C879&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/beethoven-by-josef-willibrord-maehler-circa-1804-1805_print?curator=brainpicker)

Beethoven by Josef Willibrord Mähler circa 1804-1805. (Available as [a print](https://society6.com/product/beethoven-by-josef-willibrord-maehler-circa-1804-1805_print?curator=brainpicker).)

As a teenager, while auditing Kant’s lectures at the University of Bonn, Beethoven had fallen under the spell of transcendental idealism and the ideas of the Enlightenment — ideas permeating the poetry of Friedrich Schiller. A volume of it became the young Beethoven’s most cherished book and so began the dream of setting it to music. (There is singular magic in [a timeless poem set to music](https://vimeo.com/673019873).)

One particular poem especially entranced him: Written when Beethoven was fifteen and the electric spirit of revolution saturated Europe’s atmosphere, Schiller’s “Ode to Joy” was at heart an ode to freedom — a blazing manifesto for the Enlightenment ethos that if freedom, justice, and human happiness are placed at the center of life and made its primary devotion, politically and personally, then peace and kindness would envelop humankind as an inevitable consequence. A “kiss for the whole world,” Schiller had written, and the teenage Beethoven longed to be lips of the possible.

This Elysian dream ended not even a decade later as the Reign of Terror dropped the blade of the guillotine upon Marie Antoinette, then upon ten thousand other heads and the dreams they carried. Schiller died considering his “Ode to Joy” a failure — an idealist’s fantasy unmoored from reality, a work of art that might have been of service perhaps for him, perhaps for a handful of others, “but not for the world.”

The young Beethoven was among those few it touched, and this was enough, more than enough — he took Schiller’s bright beam of possibility and magnified it through the lens of his own genius to illuminate all of humanity for all of time. Epochs later, in the savage century of the World Wars and the Holocaust, Rebecca West — another uncommon visionary, who understood that [“art is not a plaything, but a necessity”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/03/15/rebecca-west-art/) — would contemplate [how those rare few help the rest of humanity endure](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/02/24/rebecca-west-black-lamb-grey-falcon/), observing that “if during the next million generations there is but one human being born in every generation who will not cease to inquire into the nature of his fate, even while it strips and bludgeons him, some day we shall read the riddle of our universe.”

While Schiller’s poem was ripening in Beethoven’s imagination, the decade-long Napoleonic Wars stripped and bludgeoned Europe. When Napoleon’s armies invaded and occupied Vienna — where Beethoven had moved at twenty-one to study with his great musical hero, Haydn — most of the wealthy fled to the country. He took refuge with his brother, sister-in-law, and young nephew in the city. Thirty-nine and almost entirely deaf, Beethoven found himself “suffering misery in a most concentrated form” — misery that “affected both body and soul” so profoundly that he produced “very little coherent work.” From inside the vortex of uncertainty and suffering, he wrote:

> The existence I had built up only a short time ago rests on shaky foundations. What a destructive, disorderly life I see and hear around me: nothing but drums, cannons, and human misery in every form.

That spring, Haydn’s death only deepened his despair at life. The next six years were an unremitting heartache. His love [went unreturned](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/10/12/immortal-beloved-beethoven-love-letters/). He grew estranged from one of his brothers, who married a woman Beethoven disliked. His other brother died. He entered an endless legal combat over guardianship of his young nephew. He spent a year bedridden with a mysterious illness he called “an inflammatory fever,” riddled with skull-splitting headaches. His hearing almost completely deteriorated. He grew repulsed by the trendy mysticism of new musical developments, which made no room for the raw human emotion that was to him both the truest material and truest product of art.

[![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2012/04/blake_bookofjob_music_small.jpg?resize=680%2C577&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/job-and-his-family-restored-to-prosperity-by-william-blake-1805_print?sku=s6-21832017p4a1v1?curator=brainpicker)

One of William Blake’s paintings for _The Book of Job_, 1806. (Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/job-and-his-family-restored-to-prosperity-by-william-blake-1805_print?sku=s6-21832017p4a1v1?curator=brainpicker).)

Somehow, he kept composing, the act itself becoming the fulcrum by which Beethoven lifted himself out of the black hole to perch on the event horizon of a new period of great creative fertility. While Blake — [his twin in the tragic genius of outsiderdom](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/08/08/aldred-kazin-william-blake-beethoven/) — was painting the music of the heavens, Beethoven was grounding a possible heaven onto a disillusioned earth with music.

And then he ended up in jail.

One autumn day in 1822, the fifty-two-year-old composer put on his moth-eaten coat and set out for what he intended as a short morning walk in the city, his mind a tempest of ideas. Walking had always been [his primary laboratory for creative problem-solving](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/11/25/beethoven-on-creativity/), so the morning stroll unspooled into a long half-conscious walk along the Danube. In a classic manifestation of the self-forgetting that marks the intense creative state now known as [“flow,”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/12/05/peter-turchi-a-muse-a-maze-book-flow/) Beethoven lost track of time, of distance, of the demands of his own body.

![Image 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/beethoven_JuliusSchmid.jpg?resize=680%2C435&ssl=1)

Beethoven by Julius Schmid

He walked and walked, hatless and absorbed, not realizing how famished and fatigued he was growing, until the afternoon found him wandering disheveled and disoriented in a river basin far into the countryside. There, he was arrested by local police for “behaving in a suspicious manner,” taken to jail as “a tramp” with no identity papers, and mocked for claiming that he was the great Beethoven — by then a national icon, with a corpus of celebrated concertos and sonatas to his name, and eight whole symphonies.

The tramp raged and raged, until eventually, close to midnight, the police dispatched a nervous officer to wake up a local musical director, who Beethoven demanded could identify him. Instant recognition. Righteous rage. Apologies. Immediate release. More rage. More apologies. Beethoven spent the night at his liberator’s house. In the morning, the town’s apologetic mayor collected him and drove him back to Vienna in the mayoral carriage.

What had so distracted Beethoven from space and time and self was that, twenty-seven years after falling under the spell of Schiller’s poem, he was at last ferocious with ideas for bringing it to life in music. He had been thinking about it incessantly for months. “Ode to Joy” would become the crowning achievement of his crowning achievement — the choral finale of his ninth and final symphony. It would distill the transcendent torment of his creative life: how to integrate rage and redemption, the solace of poetry with the drama of music; how to channel his own poetic fury as a force of beauty, of vitality, of meaning; how to turn the human darkness he had witnessed and suffered into something incandescent, something superhuman.

[![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/rackham_littlebrotherlittlesister0.jpg?resize=680%2C946&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/art-by-arthur-rackham-for-the-brothers-grimm-fairy-tale-the-gnomes-1917_print?curator=brainpicker)

One of Arthur Rackham’s [rare 1917 illustrations](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/02/29/arthur-rackham-brothers-grimm/) for the fairy tales of the Brothers Grimm. (Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/art-by-arthur-rackham-for-the-brothers-grimm-fairy-tale-the-gnomes-1917_print?curator=brainpicker).)

It had to be in a symphony, although he had not composed one in a decade and no composer — not Bach, not Mozart, not his hero Haydn — had ever woven lyric poetry or any words at all into a symphony before; the word “lyrics” was yet to enter the lexicon in its musical sense. It had to be the crowning choral finale of the symphony, although he had not written much choral music before. But the light of the idea beamed bright and irrefutable as spring. This was no time for old laurels, no time for catering to proven populisms — this was the time for creation. A decade earlier, Beethoven had [written back](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/05/18/beethoven-emilie-letter/) to a young girl aspiring to become a great pianist, offering his advice on the central urgency of the creative calling:

> The true artist is not proud… Though he may be admired by others, he is sad not to have reached that point to which his better genius only appears as a distant, guiding sun.

So often, in advising others, we are advising ourselves — the most innocent, vulnerable, and visionary parts of us, those parts from which the spontaneity and daring central to creative work spring. I wonder whether Beethoven remembered his own advice to Emilie as he faced the blank page that spring in 1822 when the first radiant contours of his “Ode to Joy” filled his mind and his footfall.

By summer, he was actively seeking out commissions to live on as he labored. He managed to procure a meager £50 from London’s Harmony Society, but that was enough subsistence and assurance to get to work. For more than a year, he labored unremittingly, stumbling over creative challenge after creative challenge — the price of making anything unexampled. His greatest puzzle was how to introduce the words into the final movement and how to choose the voices that would best carry them.

Meanwhile, word was spreading in Vienna that its most beloved composer was working on something wildly ambitious — his first symphony in a decade, and no ordinary symphony. But just as theater managers began vying for the premiere, Beethoven stunned everyone with the announcement that it was going to premiere in Berlin. He gave no reason. Viennese musicians took it as an affront — did he think they were too traditional to appreciate something so bold? He had been born in Germany, yes, but he had become himself in Austria. Surely, he owed the seedbed of his creative blossoming some measure of faith.

At the harsh peak of winter, Karoline Unger — the nineteen-year-old contralto Beethoven had already chosen to voice the deepest feeling-tones of his “Ode to Joy” — exhorted him to premiere his masterwork in Vienna. Writing in his _Conversation Books_ — the notebooks through which the deaf composer communicated with the hearing world — she told him he had “too little self-confidence” in the Viennese public’s reception of his masterwork, urged him to go forward with the concert, then exclaimed: “O Obstinacy!”

![Image 5](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/karolinunger.jpg?resize=680%2C699&ssl=1)

Karolin Unger

Within a month, thirty of his most esteemed Austrian admirers — musicians and poets, composers and chamberlains — had co-written and signed an impassioned open letter to Beethoven, laced with patriotism and flattery, telling him that while his “name and creations belong to all contemporaneous humanity and every country which opens a susceptible bosom to art,” it is his artistic duty to complete the Austrian triad of Mozart and Haydn; imploring him not to entrust “the appreciation for the pure and eternally beautiful” to unworthy “foreign power” and to establish instead “a new sovereignty of the True and the Beautiful” in Vienna. The letter was hand-delivered to him by a court secretary who tutored the royal family.

Not even the most stubborn and single-minded artist is impervious to the sway of adulation. “It’s very beautiful, it makes me very happy!” The Viennese concert was on.

But Beethoven bent under the weight of his own expectations in a crippling combination of micro-managing and indecision. Eager to control every littlest detail to perfection, he committed to one theater, then changed his mind and committed to another, then it all became too much to bear — he cancelled the concert altogether.

After a monthlong tailspin, the finitude of time — concert season was almost over — pinned him to the still point of decision. He uncancelled the concert and, once again confounding everyone, signed with one of the underbidding imperial court theaters he had at first rejected.

The date was set for early May. He hand-picked the four soloists who would anchor the choir and assembled an orchestra dwarfing all convention: two dozen violins, two dozen wind instruments, a dozen cellos and basses, ten violas, and all that percussion.

It was to be not only a performance, not only a premiere, but something more — the emblem of a credo, musical and humanistic. The reception of the symphony would make or break the reception of the ideals behind it. Against this backdrop, it is slightly less shocking — but only slightly — that, in an astonishing final bid for total control of his creation, Beethoven demanded that he conduct the symphony himself.

Everyone knew he was deaf. Now they feared he was demented.

[![Image 6](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2015/10/beethoven.jpg?w=680&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Thayers-Life-Beethoven-2-Volumes/dp/069109103X/?tag=braipick-20)

Beethoven by Joseph Karl Stieler

The theater, having won the coveted premiere, reluctantly conceded, fearing Beethoven might change his mind again if his demand went unmet, but persuaded him to have the original conductor onstage with him, with every assurance that he would only be there for backup. The conductor, meanwhile, instructed the choir and orchestra to follow only his motions and “pay no attention whatever to Beethoven’s beating of the time.” The best assurance even one of Beethoven’s closest friends — who later became his biographer — could muster was that the theater would be too dim for anyone to notice that Beethoven was conducting in his old green frock and not in the fashionable black coat a conductor was supposed to wear.

After two catastrophic rehearsals — the only two the enormous ensemble could manage in the brief time before the performance — the soloists railed that their parts were simply impossible to sing. Karoline Unger called him a “tyrant over all the vocal organs.” One of the two male soloists quit altogether and had to be replaced by a member of the choir who had memorized the part.

Somehow, the show went on.

On the early evening of May 7, 1824, the Viennese crowded into the concert hall — but they were not the usual patrons. Looking up to the royal box, Beethoven was crushed to see it empty. He had journeyed to the palace to personally invite the Emperor and Empress but, like most of the aristocracy, they had vanished into their country estate as soon as spring broke the harsh Austrian winter. He was going to be playing for the people. But it was the people, after all, that Schiller had yearned to vitalize with his poem.

Beethoven walked onto the grand stage, faced the orchestra, and raised his arms. Despite the natural imperfections of a performance built on such tensions, something shifted as soon as the music — exalted, sublime, total — rose above the individual lives and their individual strife, subsuming every body and every soul in a single harmonious transcendence.

After the final chord of “Ode to Joy” resounded, the gasping silence broke into a scream of applause. People leapt to their feet, waving their handkerchiefs and chanting his name. Beethoven, still facing the orchestra and still waving his arms to the delayed internal time of music only he could hear, noticed none of it, until Karoline Unger stood up, took his arm, and gently turned him around.

With the birth of photography still [fifteen years of trial and triumph away](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/04/03/virginia-woolf-julia-margaret-cameron-photography/), it is only in the mind’s eye that one can picture the cascade of confusion, disbelief, and elation that must have washed over Beethoven’s face in that sublime moment when his guiding sun seemed suddenly so proximate, almost blinding with triumph.

As soon as he faced the audience, the entire human mass erupted with not one, not two, not three, but four volcanic bursts of applause, until the Police Commissioner managed to yell “Silence!” over the fifth. These were still revolutionary times, after all, and art that roused so fierce a response in the human soul — even if that response was exultant joy — was dangerous art. Here, in the unassailable message of “Ode to Joy,” was a clarion call to humanity to discard all the false gods that had fueled a century of unremitting wars and millennia of inequality — the divisions of nation and rank, the oppressions of dogma and tradition — and band together in universal sympathy and solidarity.

[![Image 7](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/vanessabell_stringquartet_virginiawoolf.jpg?resize=680%2C907&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/woodcut-by-vanessa-bell-from-a-string-quartet-by-virginia-woolf-1921_print?curator=brainpicker)

Woodcut by Vanessa Bell from “A String Quartet” by Virginia Woolf, 1921. (Available as [a print](https://society6.com/product/woodcut-by-vanessa-bell-from-a-string-quartet-by-virginia-woolf-1921_print?curator=brainpicker).)

The sound of Beethoven’s call resounded long after its creator was gone. Whitman celebrated it as [the profoundest expression of nature and human nature](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/11/17/walt-whitman-specimen-days-music/). Helen Keller “heard” it with her hand pressed against the radio speaker and [suddenly understood the meaning of music](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/10/11/helen-keller-beethoven-letter/). Chilean protesters sang it as they took down the Pinochet dictatorship. Japanese musicians performed it after the Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami. Chinese students blasted it in Tiananmen Square. Leonard Bernstein, [patron saint of music as an instrument of humanism](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/11/25/leonard-bernstein-jfk-speech/), conducted a group of musicians who had lived on both sides of the Berlin Wall in a Christmas Day concert after its fall. Ukrainian composer Victoria Poleva reimagined it for an international concert commemorating the fiftieth anniversary. A decade later, the National Symphony Orchestra of Ukraine performed her reimagining not long before a twenty-first century tyrant with a Napoleonic complex and a soul deaf to the music of life bludgeoned the small country with his lust for power.

But this, I suspect, was Beethoven’s stubborn, sacred point — the reason he never gave up on Schiller’s dream, even as he lived through nightmares: this unassailable insistence that although the Napoleons and Putins of the world will rise to power again and again over the centuries, they will also fall, because there is something in us more powerful as long as we continue placing freedom, justice, and universal happiness at the center of our commitment to life, even as we live through nightmares. Two centuries after Beethoven, Zadie Smith affirmed this elemental reality in her own life-honed conviction that [“progress is never permanent, will always be threatened, must be redoubled, restated and reimagined if it is to survive.”](https://www.themarginalian.org/2018/02/08/zadie-smith-feel-free-optimism-and-despair/)

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=B_5z0m7cs0A)

In the winter of my thirteenth year, two centuries after Beethoven’s day and a few fragile years after the fall of Bulgaria’s communist dictatorship, I stood in the holiday-bedazzled National Symphony Hall alongside a dozen classmates from the Sofia Mathematics Gymnasium, our choir about to perform Beethoven’s “Ode to Joy,” recently adopted as the anthem of Europe by the European Union, of which the newly liberated Bulgaria longed to be a part.

We sang the lyrics in Bulgarian, but “joy” has no direct translation. “Felicity” might come the closest, or “mirth” — those wing-clipped cousins of joy, bearing the same bright feeling-tone, but lacking its elation, its all-pervading exhale — a diminishment reflecting the spirit of a people just emerging from five centuries of Ottoman occupation closely followed by a half-century Communist dictatorship.

And yet we stood there in our best clothes, in the spring of life, singing together, our teenage minds abloom with quadratic equations and a lust for life, our teenage bodies reverberating with the redemptive dream of a visionary who had died epochs before any of our lives was but a glimmer in a great-great-grandparent’s eye, our teenage spirits longing to kiss the whole world with possibility.

Today, “Ode to Joy” — a recording by the Berlin Philharmonic from the year I was born — streams into my wireless headphones as I cross the Brooklyn Bridge on my bicycle, riding into a life undreamt in that teenage girl’s wildest dreams, into a world unimaginable to Beethoven, a world where suffering remains our constant companion but life is infinitely more possible for infinitely more people, and more kinds of people, than even the farthest seer of 1822 could have envisioned.

I ride into the spring night, singing. This, in the end, might be the truest translation of “joy” — this ecstatic fusion of presence and possibility.

title: The Promise of Polymaths
content:
> Academia neglects interdisciplinary work that combines insights from multiple areas. Each field has expert versions which experts use among themselves, and public versions seen by outsiders, and people in field B won’t accept your using the expert version of A if that differs from the non-expert version of A that B folks have in mind. Also, if you hold an academic event on the topic of A intersect B, you’ll usually invite the most prestigious people you can get in A, and in B, but you won’t usually invite people who have specialized in A intersect B, as they will tend to be less prestigious. Thus humanity’s beliefs on many important topics have long been just inconsistent and incoherent across disparate fields of inquiry. Creating a huge opportunity to learn lots of big stuff fast: search for more contradictions between fields, and resolve them. ([More](https://www.overcomingbias.com/p/the-promise-of-polymath-llms))

Here’s a pattern that I think I see: when intellectuals and academics use the same set of standard abstractions, and analysis tools built on those abstractions, then the top folks who have most mastered these tend to agree on their application. That is, they agree on what those concepts and tools, as applied well, suggest on particular topics.

Yes, conclusions often don’t rely entirely on such tools, as analysts add in other considerations, including strong priors. And yes, less than top people disagree more often on how to apply standard tools, especially when such tools are weak. Thus it seems to me that our deepest disagreements are due to a great degree to our using different sets of abstractions and tools, sets which often suggest conflicting conclusions in simple first pass analyses.

This seems confirmed by the fact that the rare polymaths who have mastered the same multiple sets of relevant abstractions also tend to agree more, even though they agree less than those who master only one standard set of abstractions (and related tools). More disagreement here is plausible, as, to apply multiple sets of abstractions, you’ll need to think about how to integrate them into a unified analytical framework, and if there is no standard way to do that, different polymaths may do that differently.

Thus most of our deep disagreements might be resolved if we could find ways to induce more people to learn multiple relevant sets of abstractions, to then listen more to them, and to get them to work more on agreeing on how to best integrate them. We don’t do this now due to the low status described above on interdisciplinary work.

Now, yes, it is easier for big disciplines to agree on who is best, and thus to reward people for being good. It seems at first glance harder to do this for a world of polymaths working on many different if overlapping sets of abstractions. But I can think of some ideas without much effort, and this seems a problem well worth working on.

Yes, even if we gave polymaths proper respect, and good evaluate them well, there’d still be lots of lower-quality analysis, and disagreement due to differing priors. But when top people came to focus on deep questions, we’d agree and be right a lot more.

# UAP Disclosure Wouldn’t Crash Society

[![Image 2: Robin Hanson's avatar](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1ME6!,w_36,h_36,c_fill,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fde4f2447-696c-4204-bb8e-0ed611a5d2d3_2403x3600.jpeg)](https://substack.com/@wildideaman)

In the past, authorities have authorized censorship on the basis of claims of substantial chances of social disruption or collapse if people were free to hear about religious heresy, alternate ideologies, sexually permissive art, losses in ongoing wars, looming disasters, and pandemic details. Quite often, those who pushed for such censorship benefited from it in ways well beyond the prevention of social collapse.

Some say that the US govt has long known of strong evidence that some UFOs/UAPs are aliens, but has shied away from disclosing this to the public out of fears that it might induce big social disruptions, such as riots or market crashes. Others call this a sensible fear, and call for careful study and elaborate plans before disclosure.

This all just seems quite wrong to me. First, people are mostly calm and orderly, even in huge disasters like the sinking of the Titanic. They may riot to express their anger, but not due to learning of some new scientific result. Relativity and quantum mechanics induced quite radical changes to our concepts, but led to no riots I know of.

Second, most of us are focused on the details of our lives, and not much moved unless the larger world makes a big effort to call something out there to our attention. And learning that some UFOs are aliens just doesn’t seem to imply much different for most lives. It is only a tiny fraction of us for whom our related abstract opinions might matter enough to us to make this revelation deeply disturbing.

Third, if in fact aliens have been visiting Earth for many decades, or even centuries, then they pretty clearly have long had the option to destroy us, intervene in our world, or clearly reveal themselves, options that they just have not much taken. They have also not been building or changing much near Earth, at least that we can see. Aliens aren’t trading much with humans, and any alien tech that humans have come across has clearly not given those humans much of a tech advantage.

So unless aliens plans are in some strange way sharply conditional on human elites coming to openly admit their existence, I see little reason why learning that some UFOs are aliens should change much. Aliens would mostly just continue to ignore us, and reveal too little to be of much use. Just as in prior decades. (A [poll](https://x.com/robinhanson/status/2116983779814207564) agrees.)

There might be much bigger consequences for human elites who previously ridiculed the idea of UFOs as aliens, and for human governments shown to have lied about UFOs. Those parties do indeed have selfish reasons to prevent disclosure.
